summary: For 9–10 year-olds learning prime, prime factor and composite numbers: establish whether a number up to 100 is prime and recall the primes to 19. Primeness is grounded on factor-finding — a prime is a number whose only rectangle is 1×n (exactly two factors: 1 and itself); composite has more than two; 1 is neither because it has only one factor. Learners build this through rectangle-building, the Sieve of Eratosthenes, efficient square-root-bounded divisibility testing, and justified classification (e.g. 51 = 3×17 → composite), with checkable recall and reasoning to confirm the definition they actually hold.
misconceptions: Believing 1 is prime (it has only one factor — it is neither).
Thinking all odd numbers are prime (9, 15, 21, 51 are composite) or that 2 isn't prime because it's even.
Checking divisibility inefficiently (testing all numbers, not just primes to the square root).
Confusing 'prime factor' with 'factor' — not every factor is prime.

activities.title: Rectangle-building: when is only 1×n possible?
steps: Take a number and try to arrange that many counters (or squares on grid paper) into complete rectangles with more than one row and more than one column (a single line, 1×n, does not count as another rectangle).
For 51, find that a 3×17 rectangle can be built, so 51 has factors other than 1 and itself — it is composite.

For 97, try rows of 2, 3, 5 and 7 — the primes up to its square root (just under 10), since any larger factor would pair with a smaller one already tested — and find that only a single 1×97 line forms, so 97 is prime.
Try the number 1: it forms only a single 1×1 square — one factor — so it fits neither the prime nor the composite group.
Record each verdict with its factor pair as justification (e.g. '51 = 3×17, composite'; '97, only 1×97, prime').
activities.insight: A prime number can only be made into the 1×n rectangle (exactly two factors); a composite makes at least one other rectangle; and 1 is neither prime nor composite because it has only a single factor.

activities.title: Sieve of Eratosthenes on a hundred square
steps: On a 1–100 grid, first cross out 1 (it is neither prime nor composite), then circle 2 and cross out every later multiple of 2.
Move to the next uncrossed number (3) and cross out its multiples; repeat for 5, then 7.

Notice that the numbers still standing (circled or uncrossed) are exactly the primes, and that every number crossed out as a multiple is a multiple of a smaller prime, so it is composite (1 was crossed out separately because it is neither).
Highlight the primes up to 19 (2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19) for memorisation.
activities.insight: Composite numbers are exactly the multiples that get crossed out; once 1 is set aside as neither, the survivors are the primes. This also makes the primes to 19 visible for recall.

activities.title: Efficient primality testing to the square root
steps: To test whether a whole number greater than 1 is prime, divide only by the primes 2, 3, 5, 7… up to its square root (1 is neither prime nor composite, so it is not tested this way).
Use divisibility shortcuts: even → ÷2; digit sum divisible by 3 → ÷3; ends in 0 or 5 → ÷5.
Test 97: not even, digit sum 16 (not divisible by 3), does not end in 0/5, not divisible by 7 — and since the next prime 11 has 11×11 = 121 > 97, there is no need to test further, so 97 is prime.
Test 51: digit sum 5+1 = 6, divisible by 3, so 51 = 3×17 → composite.
activities.insight: For a whole number greater than 1, you only need to check divisibility by primes up to the square root; if none divide the number, it is prime. Divisibility rules make this fast.

activities.title: Classify and justify, including the tricky cases
steps: Sort numbers into three groups: prime, composite, and neither — placing 1 in 'neither'.
Decide whether 51 is prime or composite and justify using a factor pair (51 = 3×17 → composite).
Explain why 2 is prime (exactly two factors) even though it is even, and why 9, 15, 21 and 51 are composite even though they are odd.
List all primes up to 19 from memory and state for each why it is prime.
activities.insight: Classification requires checking factors, not 'feel': parity does not decide primeness, 1 is neither, and every classification needs a factor justification.

activities.title: Prove it: Socratic justification challenge
steps: Respond to the question 'How could you prove 97 is prime without checking every number below it?' by describing which divisors you need to test and why.
Explain in your own words why 1 is neither prime nor composite.
Argue whether a classmate who called 51 prime is right, and show the check that settles it.
activities.insight: Being able to articulate and defend the reasoning — which divisors to test, why 1 is neither, how to catch a false positive like 51 — shows the definition is genuinely held.

checkQuestion: Is 51 a prime number or a composite number? Decide, and then explain how you know — what makes a number prime, and what did you check for 51?
checkAnswer: 51 is composite, not prime, because it has factors other than 1 and itself: 51 = 3 × 17. A child reasoning correctly defines prime as having EXACTLY two factors (1 and itself) and shows 51 fails because 3 divides it.
